Last year our tracing costs tripled in six months, while request volume grew maybe twenty percent.
The reason was simple. Every team turned on OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation and we kept one hundred percent of spans.
So the first thing everyone does is head-based sampling. You decide at the start of a request whether to keep the trace.
We set head sampling to ten percent in the SDK. Costs dropped immediately. Everyone was happy for about a week.
Then we had an incident, and the traces for the failing requests were gone. Ninety percent of them were dropped before we knew they would fail.
That's the core problem with head sampling. You decide before you know whether the trace is interesting.
Tail-based sampling flips that. The collector waits until the whole trace has arrived, then decides whether to keep it.
So you can write a policy like: keep every trace that has an error, keep every trace slower than two seconds, and keep one percent of everything else.
In the OpenTelemetry Collector that's the tail sampling processor. You give it a list of policies and a decision wait time.
Decision wait is how long the collector buffers spans for a trace before deciding. We use ten seconds.
Here is the part that bit us. Tail sampling only works if all spans of a trace reach the same collector instance.
If you just put a normal load balancer in front of three collectors, the spans of one trace get scattered, and no collector sees the full trace.
The fix is a two-layer setup. A first layer of collectors runs the load balancing exporter, which routes by trace ID.
The second layer runs tail sampling. Every span of a trace lands on the same instance because the routing key is the trace ID.
Now, memory. Tail sampling holds traces in memory during the decision wait. More traffic times longer wait equals more memory.
Our collectors started getting OOM killed at peak. We fixed it with the memory limiter processor and by setting num traces to a real number.
Put the memory limiter first in the pipeline. It refuses new data before the process runs out of memory, instead of crashing.
With all of that in place we keep one hundred percent of error traces, about eight percent of total volume, and the bill went down sixty percent.
One more thing people ask: what about metrics? Generate your RED metrics from spans before sampling, with the span metrics connector.
That way your dashboards and SLOs see all the traffic, even though you only store a fraction of the traces.
Let me show you the actual policy file we run in production. The first policy is status code error. The second is latency over two thousand milliseconds.
The third is a probabilistic policy at one percent, so we still have a baseline of healthy traces to compare against.
And we added a fourth policy for rare endpoints, like the payments refund API, where we keep everything because the volume is tiny.
If you're starting tomorrow: move sampling decisions to the collector, route by trace ID, and put the memory limiter first.
